The Bushveld gerbil (Gerbilliscus leucogaster) exhibits a basal metabolic rate that has been quantified through respirometry trials conducted under stable thermal conditions. When measured at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the resting oxygen consumption of this species reaches approximately 132.5 milliliters per hour [JOi = approximately 132.5 milliliters per hour], a value that aligns with the typical metabolic scaling observed in similarly sized murine rodents. This relatively elevated metabolic demand is consistent with the energetic requirements of an omnivorous, semi-arid adapted species that forages extensively for seeds and invertebrates. The females of this species attain an adult body mass that can reach up to 132.5 grams [Wwi = up to 132.5 grams], representing the upper end of the size range documented in field populations, which typically spans from 32 to 114 grams. This substantial body mass is partly attributable to the accumulation of fat reserves that buffer against seasonal food scarcity in their savanna and woodland habitats.

Reproductive output in Gerbilliscus leucogaster has been characterised through captive breeding studies that carefully controlled thermal conditions. Under a constant ambient temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], females produce litters containing approximately 3.9 pups [N_R_i = litters containing approximately 3.9 pups] and can generate approximately 5 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 5 litters per year], a reproductive schedule that reflects the species' capacity for rapid population growth in favourable environments. The neonates themselves are born at a remarkably low mass, weighing only 4.5 grams [Wwb = 4.5 grams] at birth, which is typical for altricial rodents that undergo extensive post-natal development. This modest birth mass is consistent with values reported for the congeneric Gerbilliscus afra and requires a substantial investment of maternal resources during the ensuing lactation period.

Gestation in the Bushveld gerbil is notably brief, a common trait among small-bodied murid rodents adapted to unpredictable environments where rapid turnover is advantageous. The gestation period lasts 28 days [tg = 28 days] when females are maintained at a thermoneutral temperature of 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C], a duration that allows for multiple litters within a single breeding season. This short intrauterine phase is followed by an extended period of post-natal dependency, with the young suckling from their mother until they are fully weaned. Weaning occurs at 28 days after birth [tx = 28 days after birth], a milestone that coincides with the onset of solid food consumption, and is observed at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], at which point the juveniles begin to transition to solid foods and become increasingly independent of maternal provisioning.

The developmental trajectory from birth to reproductive maturity in Gerbilliscus leucogaster involves several distinct physiological milestones. Young gerbils experience a gradual process of somatic growth and gonadal maturation, culminating in the attainment of sexual maturity. Based on data available from closely related species such as Gerbilliscus afra, puberty is estimated to occur at 152 days after birth [tp = 152 days after birth] under a constant ambient temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. This relatively prolonged juvenile phase, lasting approximately five months, is thought to reflect the time required for individuals to reach the critical body size necessary for successful reproduction and to establish the fat reserves that enhance overwinter survival in their semi-arid habitats.

Longevity records for the Bushveld gerbil are limited, but comparative life-history data from the congeneric Gerbilliscus afra provide a useful benchmark for estimating maximum lifespan. When maintained under stable captive conditions at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], individuals can survive for up to 5.7 years [am = up to 5.7 years], a duration that is relatively extended for a rodent of this small body size and which aligns with a life-history strategy characterised by high fecundity and moderate iteroparity. This lifespan allows for multiple reproductive bouts over the course of an individual's life, thereby compensating for the high rates of juvenile mortality that are typical in unpredictable savanna ecosystems. In wild populations, predation pressure and seasonal resource limitations likely reduce actual longevity considerably below this captive maximum.
